scenes.heading: Concurrency Pattern: Pipelines
scenes.narration: In the next minute, let's build a mental model of Go pipelines: a chain of concurrent stages connected by channels.

scenes.heading: What a pipeline is
items: Each stage receives, transforms, and sends on channels
Stages run concurrently, streaming data end to end
The sender owns and closes its own output channel
scenes.narration: A pipeline stage is a small function: it receives values on an inbound channel, transforms them, and sends them on an outbound channel that it owns and closes. Because every stage runs in its own goroutine, data streams through the whole chain at once. The two rules that keep it correct are sender-closes, meaning a stage closes only its output and never its input, and cancellation, so an early-exiting consumer never strands the goroutines upstream.

scenes.heading: Leak-safe shutdown
steps: Wire stages by nesting channel functions
Source closes first; the close cascades down
Or the consumer cancels the context early
Every stage's select on Done() lets it exit
scenes.narration: Compose stages by passing one stage's output as the next stage's input. They stream concurrently, so item one flows downstream while item two is produced upstream. Termination happens one of two ways: the source closes its output, and that close cascades down each stage's range; or the consumer stops early and cancels the context, and every stage's select on ctx.Done lets a blocked send abandon and return.

scenes.heading: A cancellable stage
scenes.narration: This stage shows both discipline rules. The deferred close guarantees the output channel closes on every exit path. The range over the input ends naturally when the upstream closes it. And the send is wrapped in a select on ctx.Done, so if the consumer cancels while this stage is blocked on a send, it returns immediately instead of blocking forever. That select is the single most important line for preventing early-exit leaks.

scenes.text: Throughput equals the slowest stage — fan it out. Keep buffers shallow so backpressure surfaces instead of hoarding memory.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: a pipeline's throughput is gated by its slowest stage, so parallelize that bottleneck by fanning it out across workers. Keep inter-stage buffers shallow so a slow stage pushes back on the fast ones rather than piling up in memory, and always thread a context through so shutdown is leak-free.
